blocks.text:
Use it once you have booked a Level I window: the next ones are February and May 2027. The exam is 180 questions over 4 hours 30 minutes, and CFA Institute suggests 300+ hours of study.[^cfa] The August 2026 pass rate was 43%, so more than half of candidates did not pass.[^cfa]

Most failed attempts we see come from two problems. Candidates spend their hours on the topics they enjoy rather than the ones the exam rewards, and they memorise formulas they have never seen work on a real number. This plan fixes the first with exam-weight ordering and the second with live market data.
The framework: weight first, then live data

Three rules shape the 12 weeks:

1. **Order by weight and dependency.** Quantitative Methods comes first because Fixed Income, Equities and Portfolio Construction all lean on it. Financial Statement Analysis gets two weeks because it is both heavily weighted and long.
2. **Ethics goes late, then comes back.** At 10–15% it is the heaviest topic and the most memory-based, so it is studied in week 10 and reviewed again in week 12.
3. **Every topic gets one live-market exercise.** Each week you take one formula and run it on numbers from this month: an index, a Treasury bill, a volatility index. A formula you have seen move is a formula you can rebuild under exam pressure.

The full curriculum weights are on our [CFA Level I course page](/courses/cfa-level-i), and our free [CFA Level I Exam Map](/resources) puts them on one printable page.

blocks.text:
1. **Days 1–3: read and summarise.** One pass through the reading, writing every formula on a single sheet.
2. **Day 4: the live-market exercise.** Pull this week's real numbers and work the formula by hand, then in a spreadsheet. Write one sentence on what the answer means.
3. **Days 5–6: questions.** End-of-chapter and question-bank items, timed at 90 seconds each.
4. **Day 7: review the errors.** Each wrong answer goes in an error log with its cause: concept, formula or reading the question too fast.
Worked example: one month of real data

This is what week 1, week 7 and week 8 look like on real numbers. We use the S&P 500 from 10 September to 9 October 2026: 22 trading days, so 21 daily returns.[^spx]

**Week 1, Quantitative Methods.** The index moved from 7,591.70 to 7,811.54. The holding-period return is $7{,}811.54 / 7{,}591.70 - 1 = 2.90\%$. The 21 daily returns average 0.138% with a sample standard deviation of 0.633%. Scaled to a year, that is about 10.05% volatility. Ten of the 21 days were up, and the largest one-day moves were +1.49% and −0.77%.

blocks.title: S&P 500 daily close, 10 Sep – 9 Oct 2026
blocks.methodology: Daily closing levels for the 22 US trading days from 10 September to 9 October 2026. These are price levels: dividends are not included.
blocks.limitations: One month of data is enough to practise the formulas, not to estimate long-run volatility. A price index understates total return because it leaves out dividends.
blocks.alt: The S&P 500 rose from 7,591.70 to 7,811.54 over the month, a 2.90% gain, with small daily swings.
blocks.caption: The month we use for the week-1 and week-8 exercises.

blocks.explanation: σ daily is the sample standard deviation of daily returns. 252 is the usual number of trading days in a year. Volatility scales with the square root of time because, if returns are independent, variances add up over time.

blocks.text:
**Week 7, Fixed Income.** On 8 October 2026 the 3-month US T-bill was quoted at a 4.05% discount rate.[^fred] For 91 days on a 100 face value:

- Price: $100 \times (1 - 0.0405 \times 91/360) = 98.976$
- Holding-period yield: $100 / 98.976 - 1 = 1.034\%$
- Money market yield (360-day basis): 4.09%
- Bond-equivalent yield (365-day basis): 4.15%

One bill, four different-looking rates. That is exactly the kind of question Level I asks, and seeing it on a real quote is how it stops being confusing. The quote also rose from 3.81% a month earlier, a 24 basis-point move that you can reuse in week 2 to talk about rate expectations.

**Week 8, Derivatives and Risk Management.** On 9 October the VIX closed at 14.84.[^vix] The VIX is the market's expected volatility for the next 30 days, quoted as an annual percentage, so it implies about $14.84\% / \sqrt{252} \approx 0.93\%$ per day. The S&P 500's realised volatility over the previous month was 10.05%. Option buyers were paying for more volatility than had recently happened, which is normal: implied volatility usually sits above realised. Over the same month the VIX fell from 17.84 as the index rose 2.90%, a live look at the negative link between volatility and equity prices.

blocks.title: Check the week-1 numbers yourself
blocks.code:
import statistics as st
from math import sqrt

close = [7591.70, 7656.98, 7619.98, 7585.73, 7551.81, 7637.76, 7650.50,
         7764.70, 7764.64, 7706.03, 7704.13, 7743.41, 7683.69, 7670.84,
         7651.54, 7666.45, 7722.72, 7773.95, 7818.93, 7801.77, 7765.36, 7811.54]

r = [close[i] / close[i - 1] - 1 for i in range(1, len(close))]
print(f"Holding-period return: {close[-1] / close[0] - 1:.2%}")
print(f"Mean daily return:     {st.mean(r):.3%}")
print(f"Daily volatility:      {st.stdev(r):.3%}")
print(f"Annualised volatility: {st.stdev(r) * sqrt(252):.2%}")
blocks.explanation: Turns 22 daily closes into 21 simple returns, then prints the holding-period return, the mean and sample standard deviation of daily returns, and annualised volatility using the square-root-of-time rule.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
- **Studying Ethics first.** It is the heaviest topic, and by exam day the details are gone. Study it late and review it twice.
- **Reading without questions.** Reading feels productive, but marks come from questions. Aim for at least a third of your hours on practice.
- **Mixing up the T-bill yields.** Discount rate, holding-period yield, money market yield and bond-equivalent yield are four different numbers for the same bill. Know which one the question gives you.
- **Annualising with the wrong time unit.** Daily volatility scales by √252, not by 252.
- **Skipping mock exams.** Four full timed mocks in the last two weeks build exam stamina. Doing more chapters does not.

Twelve weeks at 25 hours suits candidates with a finance degree or plenty of free time. Working professionals should stretch the same order over 16–20 weeks. One month of market data is for practising formulas, not for drawing investment conclusions, and the live numbers will be different when you study. That is deliberate: rerun each exercise on the latest data. The exam tests the CFA Institute curriculum, so live data supplements the official readings and question bank and does not replace them.

items.q: How many hours do I need for CFA Level I?
items.a: CFA Institute suggests 300+ hours. This plan budgets about 300: 12 weeks at 25 hours, or 20 weeks at 15 hours if you work full time.

items.q: Which CFA Level I topic should I study first?
items.a: Quantitative Methods. Fixed Income, Equities and Portfolio Construction all use its return, risk and time-value tools.

items.q: Why use live market data for an exam?
items.a: Because a formula you have seen work on a real number is one you can rebuild under pressure. The exam still tests the curriculum; live data makes it stick.
